questions.stem: Using the VCE Politics definitions of global actors, which of the following is a non-state actor?
options: Greenpeace
the European Union
the World Trade Organization
the Republic of Indonesia
questions.explanation: Non-state actors include non-government organisations such as Greenpeace, transnational corporations, individuals and illegal groups. The European Union is a regional grouping and the WTO is an institution of global governance; both are made up of states.

questions.stem: Bodies such as the United Nations and the IMF count as institutions of global governance because each:
options: has global scope, has states as members and facilitates cooperation between them
has a defined territory, a permanent population and widely recognised sovereignty
pursues profit across borders through subsidiaries operating in many states
brings together states from one geographic area to pursue shared regional goals
questions.explanation: Institutions of global governance, such as the United Nations or the IMF, have global scope and states as members. A body limited to one geographic area is a regional grouping, while defined territory and recognised sovereignty describe a state.

questions.stem: Which feature most clearly makes an issue a global issue?
options: It transcends national borders, so no single state can resolve it alone
It begins inside one state and stays within that state's territory
It affects every state in the world to exactly the same degree
It is debated every year at a formal session of the UN General Assembly
questions.explanation: A global issue by its nature crosses national and regional boundaries, so its resolution needs action by many global actors. Global issues rarely affect all states equally; low-lying states, for example, face far greater climate risks than others.

questions.stem: Which of the following best captures the idea of global interconnectedness?
options: the formal merging of sovereign states into a single elected world government with its own laws
the legal obligation of every state to join the main international organisations
the tendency of states to withdraw from world trade to protect local industry
the growing links between states and peoples through trade, finance, technology and movement
questions.explanation: Interconnectedness describes the dense links of trade, investment, communication and migration that tie states and peoples together. It does not involve giving up sovereignty to a world government, and states are not legally obliged to join international organisations.

questions.stem: A banking collapse in one large economy quickly leads to falling share prices, tighter lending and rising unemployment in states on other continents. This best illustrates:
options: the failure of a regional grouping to coordinate its members' tariffs
the effect of sanctions imposed by the UN Security Council on a state
the protection that sovereignty gives states against outside shocks
contagion spreading through an interconnected global financial system
questions.explanation: Because banks, investors and markets are linked across borders, a crisis in one economy can spread rapidly to others. Sovereignty gives a state legal independence, but it offers little protection from shocks transmitted through global markets.

questions.stem: In VCE Politics, a short-term cause of a global issue is one that:
options: has shaped the issue over a period of more than a century
results from the actions of one state acting alone
could be resolved within a single electoral term
has contributed to the issue within the last 10 years
questions.explanation: The study design defines contemporary as within the last 10 years, and short-term causes are those operating in that period. Older, historical causes provide context but are not the focus of analysis.

questions.stem: The Paris Agreement and the Kyoto Protocol were both negotiated under:
options: the Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer
the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change
the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade
questions.explanation: The UNFCCC, agreed in 1992, is the framework treaty under which both the Kyoto Protocol (1997) and the Paris Agreement (2015) were negotiated. The IPCC assesses climate science but does not negotiate treaties.

questions.stem: The temperature goal of the Paris Agreement is to hold the rise in global average temperature to:
options: no more than 1°C above pre-industrial levels by the year 2030
below 2°C above 2015 levels, while pursuing efforts to limit the increase to 1°C
well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels, pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5°C
below 3°C above 1990 levels, while pursuing efforts to limit it to 2°C
questions.explanation: Article 2 of the Paris Agreement sets the goal of well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and of pursuing efforts to limit warming to 1.5°C. The baseline is pre-industrial temperatures, not 1990 or 2015.

questions.stem: Under the Paris Agreement, each party must:
options: cut its emissions by the binding percentage that the treaty sets for every party
accept fines from the UNFCCC secretariat if it fails to meet its emissions target
close all of its coal-fired power stations by a deadline set in the agreement
prepare, communicate and maintain successive nationally determined contributions
questions.explanation: The Paris Agreement obliges parties to set and regularly update their own nationally determined contributions (NDCs). The content of each target is chosen by the state itself, and there are no fines or penalties for missing it.

questions.stem: Unlike the Kyoto Protocol, the Paris Agreement:
options: imposes legally binding emissions targets on developed states and on no others
was negotiated outside the United Nations climate change framework
frees developing states from any obligation to report on their emissions
asks all parties, developed and developing, to set their own emissions targets
questions.explanation: Kyoto set binding targets only for developed states, which was one reason major developing emitters had no targets. Paris replaced this with a bottom-up model in which every party sets its own contribution.

questions.stem: The main role of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) is to:
options: assess the scientific evidence on climate change for policymakers
set binding emissions targets for each of the states that are members of it
enforce the Paris Agreement by imposing trade sanctions
fund renewable energy projects in developing states
questions.explanation: The IPCC, set up in 1988, reviews and summarises climate research in assessment reports that inform negotiations. It has no power to set targets, enforce agreements or fund projects.

questions.stem: A developing state argues that wealthy industrialised states should cut emissions faster, because they produced most of the greenhouse gases emitted in the past. This argument draws on the principle of:
options: the responsibility to protect
non-refoulement
collective security
common but differentiated responsibilities
questions.explanation: The UNFCCC recognises common but differentiated responsibilities: all states share the task of addressing climate change, but obligations differ according to historical emissions and capacity. The responsibility to protect concerns mass atrocity crimes, not emissions.

questions.stem: State A benefits from emissions cuts made by other states while making few cuts of its own, because a stable climate cannot be withheld from any state. This is an example of:
options: the free-rider problem in collective action
the security dilemma between rival states
the principle of comparative advantage
a breach of the non-proliferation norm
questions.explanation: A stable climate is a global public good, so states can enjoy its benefits without paying the costs of cutting emissions. This free-rider problem makes cooperation hard to sustain. A security dilemma arises when one state's defence build-up makes others feel less secure.

questions.stem: A large coal-exporting state pledges net zero emissions by 2050 while continuing to approve new coal mines for export. A critic would most likely argue that this shows:
options: the emissions from its exported coal already count towards its own target
economic national interests are limiting its contribution to a global solution
the Paris Agreement prohibits parties from exporting any fossil fuels abroad
its pledge has no legal force, because net zero targets breach international law
questions.explanation: The critic would argue the state is protecting export income and jobs at the expense of global emissions reductions. Under UNFCCC accounting, emissions from exported coal are counted where the coal is burned, not by the exporter, which is why the exporter's pledge can look stronger than its overall impact.

questions.stem: Why does global interconnectedness make it harder for one state to cut emissions on its own?
options: Emissions are counted only in the state that finally consumes the goods that are produced
Trade agreements under the WTO prohibit member states from placing any price on carbon emissions
Greenhouse gases released by one state remain in the atmosphere above that state alone
Emissions-intensive production can shift to states with weaker rules, known as carbon leakage
questions.explanation: If one state imposes strict climate rules, firms may move production to states with weaker rules, so global emissions may not fall. National inventories count emissions where they are produced, and greenhouse gases mix through the whole atmosphere rather than staying over one state.

questions.stem: Some states argue that emissions should be compared per person rather than in total. This argument most strongly supports the position of:
options: developed states seeking to place the burden on large developing economies
populous developing states with high total but low per-person emissions
small wealthy states with very high emissions for each of their residents
small oil-exporting states whose emissions per resident are among the highest
questions.explanation: A state with a very large population can have high total emissions while each person emits relatively little, so per-person measures favour it. Small wealthy and oil-exporting states usually have high per-person emissions, so that measure would not help their case.

questions.stem: Which evidence would most strongly support the claim that the Paris Agreement has been effective?
options: Thousands of delegates attend the annual climate conference each year
Projected warming falls over time as parties strengthen successive pledges
Almost every state in the world has signed and joined the agreement
Parties lodge their pledges on time even as most of their emissions rise
questions.explanation: Effectiveness is judged by outcomes against the agreement's goals, such as lower projected warming. Near-universal membership shows participation and legitimacy, which is tempting evidence, but it does not show that emissions or warming have actually been reduced.

questions.stem: The main role of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) is to:
options: set the official interest rates charged by the central banks of all members
promote monetary stability and lend to states facing balance of payments crises
settle trade disputes between member states through binding decisions of its panels
finance long-term infrastructure projects such as dams, roads and power grids
questions.explanation: The IMF oversees the international monetary system and provides loans to states in financial difficulty. Trade disputes are handled by the WTO, long-term development projects are mainly financed by the World Bank, and central banks set their own interest rates.

questions.stem: The World Trade Organization's main functions include:
options: lending to states that are facing balance of payments crises
setting the official exchange rates of members' currencies
coordinating the monetary policies of the world's largest economies through the G20
administering trade agreements and settling trade disputes between members
questions.explanation: The WTO administers the multilateral trade rules and runs a dispute settlement system. Lending to states in crisis is the IMF's role, and exchange rates and monetary policy are set by states themselves.

questions.stem: G20 leaders first met in 2008 to coordinate responses to the global financial crisis. As a forum, the G20 differs from the IMF because it:
options: makes no binding decisions and relies on members agreeing to act
has its own funds to lend to members facing a financial crisis
includes every member state of the United Nations as a member
can impose sanctions on members that break its agreed rules
questions.explanation: The G20 is an informal forum of major economies with no treaty, secretariat or enforcement power; its commitments depend on members carrying them out. The IMF, by contrast, is a formal institution with resources it can lend.

questions.stem: During a downturn several large economies raise tariffs to protect local industries, and their trading partners respond with tariffs of their own. This challenges the resolution of global economic instability mainly because:
options: the IMF must cancel its loans to any state that raises its tariffs
tariffs automatically strengthen the currencies of every state involved
retaliatory tariffs shrink world trade and can deepen the downturn for all
tariffs of any kind are banned outright under every WTO agreement
questions.explanation: When states retaliate against each other's tariffs, trade falls and the downturn can spread and worsen. WTO members are permitted tariffs up to their agreed bound rates, so tariffs are not banned outright.

questions.stem: A state receives an IMF loan on condition that it makes deep cuts to public spending. Mass protests follow and the government falls. This best illustrates that:
options: the IMF appoints the governments of states that borrow money from it
IMF loans are grants that a borrowing state never has to repay
the World Bank vetoed the loan and so forced the government to resign from office
loan conditions requiring austerity can produce domestic political instability
questions.explanation: IMF lending often comes with conditions, such as spending cuts, that can be unpopular and destabilising at home. The IMF does not choose governments, and its loans must be repaid.

questions.stem: After a run of financial crises, states agree to give a global body new powers to monitor bank lending across borders. This outcome most clearly represents:
options: disengagement, because states have withdrawn from global cooperation
conflict, because states have used coercion against one another
political change, through a shift in global governance arrangements
political stability, because the existing rules were left unchanged
questions.explanation: Creating new powers for a global institution changes how the issue is governed, which is political change. The states here cooperated rather than disengaging, and nothing in the scenario involves coercion.

questions.stem: The Sustainable Development Goals, adopted by all UN member states in 2015, consist of:
options: 17 goals with targets to be achieved by 2030
8 goals with targets to be achieved by 2015
17 goals that are binding treaty obligations
12 goals with targets to be achieved by 2050
questions.explanation: The 2030 Agenda sets out 17 SDGs with 169 targets. The eight goals for 2015 were the earlier Millennium Development Goals, and the SDGs are political commitments rather than a binding treaty.

questions.stem: One key difference between the SDGs and the earlier Millennium Development Goals is that the SDGs:
options: are legally binding and enforced by the International Court of Justice
focus only on economic growth rather than on social or environmental goals
were adopted by the G20 rather than by the UN General Assembly
apply to all states, developed and developing, not only to poorer ones
questions.explanation: The MDGs were aimed mainly at developing states, whereas the SDGs are universal and cover every state. The SDGs also go well beyond growth, with goals on inequality, climate and peaceful societies.

questions.stem: The long-standing UN target for official development assistance from wealthy states is:
options: 2 per cent of gross national income
0.7 per cent of gross national income
7 per cent of gross domestic product
0.07 per cent of government revenue
questions.explanation: Since 1970 the UN has asked developed states to provide official development assistance equal to 0.7 per cent of their gross national income. Most donors have not reached this target, which is one challenge to funding development.

questions.stem: A private foundation spends more each year on vaccine programs in developing states than the aid budgets of many governments. This best illustrates:
options: the significant power of non-state actors in responding to global issues
a breach of the sovereignty of the states that also give foreign aid
the legal duty of private bodies to fund the SDGs under the UN Charter
the replacement of the World Health Organization by private donors
questions.explanation: Well-funded non-state actors can shape the response to global issues such as health and development. They act voluntarily; the UN Charter places no legal duty on private bodies to fund development.

questions.stem: During a global pandemic, remittances fall, tourism collapses and a developing state diverts funds to its health system. This most directly threatens:
options: its membership of the United Nations and its General Assembly vote
its right to sign trade agreements with other members of the WTO
its legal obligations under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty
its progress towards goals such as ending poverty and quality education
questions.explanation: Lost income and diverted spending reduce what households and governments can invest in poverty reduction, schooling and other SDG targets. The study design notes that COVID-19 set back many states' progress towards the SDGs.

questions.stem: The three pillars of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) are:
options: disarmament, economic sanctions and the responsibility to protect
non-proliferation, disarmament and the peaceful use of nuclear energy
deterrence, verification and the collective self-defence of all members
non-proliferation, deterrence and a permanent ban on nuclear testing
questions.explanation: The NPT aims to stop the spread of nuclear weapons, commits nuclear-weapon states to pursue disarmament, and supports access to nuclear energy for peaceful purposes. A ban on testing is the subject of a separate treaty.

questions.stem: Under the NPT, a nuclear-weapon state is defined as one that:
options: currently holds more than 100 nuclear warheads in its arsenal
holds a permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council
has signed and ratified the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty
manufactured and exploded a nuclear device before 1 January 1967
questions.explanation: The NPT recognises as nuclear-weapon states only those that had exploded a nuclear device before 1 January 1967. These five happen to be the permanent members of the Security Council, which makes that option tempting, but a permanent seat is not the treaty's test.

questions.stem: The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) contributes to non-proliferation mainly by:
options: verifying through safeguards and inspections that nuclear material is not diverted to weapons
commanding United Nations forces that seize nuclear weapons from states breaking the treaty
issuing binding judgments in legal disputes between states that possess nuclear weapons
deciding which states are entitled to hold a permanent seat on the UN Security Council for life
questions.explanation: The IAEA applies safeguards, including inspections, to check that states' nuclear programs remain peaceful. It can report breaches to the Security Council, but it has no forces of its own and is not a court.

questions.stem: The Chemical Weapons Convention is often seen as stronger than the Biological Weapons Convention mainly because it:
options: has a verification body, the OPCW, that carries out inspections
lets states keep a small stock of chemical weapons for deterrence
applies only to the states that already possess chemical weapons
was imposed by the Security Council rather than agreed by treaty
questions.explanation: The Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons inspects facilities and oversees the destruction of stockpiles. The Biological Weapons Convention has no comparable verification body, which limits confidence that states are complying.

questions.stem: Supporters of the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (2017) say it strengthens the norm against nuclear weapons. Critics say its direct effect is limited mainly because:
options: the UN General Assembly voted to reject the treaty when it was drafted
the treaty allows nuclear testing as long as it is for peaceful purposes
the treaty applies only to chemical and biological weapons, not nuclear
a treaty binds only the states that choose to become parties to it
questions.explanation: Under international law a treaty creates obligations only for states that consent to it, so states with nuclear weapons that stay outside it are not bound. Its supporters respond that it still shapes norms and expectations over time.

questions.stem: A state refuses to give up its nuclear arsenal, arguing that the weapons stop rivals from attacking it. This perspective rests mainly on the idea of:
options: collective security
humanitarian intervention
complementarity
deterrence
questions.explanation: Deterrence holds that the threat of devastating retaliation discourages an attack. Collective security is the different idea that all states act together against any aggressor, usually through the UN.

questions.stem: Non-proliferation efforts focus on state stockpiles even where those states say they will never use their weapons. A key reason is that:
options: the ICC can prosecute any state that keeps a stockpile of these weapons
weapons or materials could be stolen by or sold to illegal non-state actors
every state holding such weapons is already under Security Council sanctions
the NPT requires every state to destroy its stockpiles within a set period
questions.explanation: The study design notes the concern that weapons of mass destruction could fall into the hands of illegal non-state actors, who are hard to deter. The ICC tries individuals, not states, and the NPT sets no destruction deadline.

questions.stem: A key weakness of international law in resolving global issues is that:
options: there is no global authority able to enforce it on every sovereign state
it applies only to issues that affect fewer than ten states at a time
it can be made only by judges of the International Court of Justice
it automatically overrides the domestic law of every state in the world
questions.explanation: International law depends largely on states consenting to it and choosing to comply, because there is no world government to enforce it. It is made mainly through treaties and state practice, not by the ICJ alone.

questions.stem: Which form of international law is binding on all UN member states, whether or not they voted for it?
options: a resolution passed by a large majority of members of the UN General Assembly
a bilateral agreement between two of the UN's largest member states
a joint declaration issued by leaders at the end of a G20 summit
a Security Council resolution adopted under Chapter VII of the UN Charter
questions.explanation: Under the UN Charter, members agree to carry out Security Council decisions, and Chapter VII resolutions can require action from all of them. General Assembly resolutions are recommendations, however large the majority.

questions.stem: A state signs a multilateral treaty, but its parliament never ratifies it. In general, the state:
options: can be prosecuted at the International Criminal Court for breaching the treaty
must suspend its membership of the United Nations until ratification occurs
is not bound by the treaty, but should not act to defeat its object and purpose
is fully bound by every obligation from the moment its leader signs the treaty
questions.explanation: Signature alone does not make a state a party; it is bound once it ratifies or otherwise consents. Under the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, a signatory should meanwhile refrain from acts that would defeat the treaty's purpose.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why state sovereignty is a challenge to resolving global issues?
options: States can decline to join, or withdraw from, agreements they see as against their interests
Sovereignty obliges every state to carry out all of the resolutions passed by the UN General Assembly
Sovereignty allows institutions of global governance to override the decisions of states
Sovereign states are legally barred from negotiating treaties with more than one partner
questions.explanation: Because states are sovereign, they decide for themselves whether to accept international obligations, and they can leave agreements. Global institutions generally act only with states' consent rather than overriding them.

questions.stem: Which response to climate change is most typical of a non-government organisation such as Greenpeace?
options: negotiating and ratifying binding emissions treaties on behalf of the states that are its members
imposing carbon tariffs on imports arriving from states with high emissions
lending money to developing states that face balance of payments crises
campaigning and direct action to pressure governments and companies to cut emissions
questions.explanation: NGOs lack legal authority, so they use advocacy, research, protest and public pressure to influence states and corporations. Ratifying treaties and imposing tariffs are actions only states can take.

questions.stem: A transnational corporation lobbies governments against a carbon price while also investing heavily in renewable energy. This best illustrates that non-state actors:
options: can be sanctioned by the Security Council for lobbying governments
can hold mixed interests that both hinder and help resolution of an issue
are bound by the Paris Agreement in exactly the same way as its parties
always act to block the resolution of global issues to protect profits
questions.explanation: A corporation's interests can be complex: it may resist costs such as a carbon price while profiting from the energy transition. Only states are parties to the Paris Agreement, so corporations are not bound by it.

questions.stem: State X withdraws from a global agreement, stops paying into the fund linked to it and stops attending negotiations, but takes no action against other states. Its response is best described as:
options: cooperation
conflict
multilateralism
disengagement
questions.explanation: Global actors' responses can take the form of cooperation, disengagement or conflict. Stepping back from an agreement without acting against others is disengagement; conflict would involve actively opposing or coercing other actors.
